explainBack.question: Why does having every prediction precomputed speed up research, and why does a variant ranked at the top of the Atlas still not tell a patient anything about their own health?
explainBack.answer: Before, each candidate DNA change required its own fresh model calculation, so triaging thousands of variants was slow; because DeepMind ran the model once over all roughly nine billion single-letter changes, a researcher can now just look up scores and rank a long list immediately. But the score only predicts a molecular effect—such as a change in how a gene message is spliced. Whether that effect really happens must be shown in cells, as with the DNM1 case where a lab assay across five cell lines confirmed twelve variants produced the longer message, and even a confirmed molecular effect is only one link in the evidence chain a clinician needs before it could inform anyone's care.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: An accurate answer must include: precomputation replacing per-variant calculation (P002), ranking as a first sorting step (P003), the prediction-then-laboratory-assay sequence (P004), and the report's own limit that scores are only part of the clinical evidence chain (P005).
explainBack.assessment: The article supports this full causal answer; every step of the chain is stated in ordinary language, so the explain-back passes.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A food-tech startup finds a public database where an AI model has precomputed 'allergenicity risk scores' for millions of possible protein sequences. Their new pea-protein ingredient scores low, and the marketing team wants to label it 'confirmed non-allergenic' and skip laboratory allergy testing before launch.
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, what should the startup actually do with the precomputed score, and what may it not claim yet?
unseenTransfer.answer: The precomputed database plays the same role as the Atlas: it lets the team instantly triage candidate proteins instead of modelling each one, so a low score is a reason to prioritize this ingredient for testing. But the score is a predicted molecular property, not an observed biological outcome. Like the DNM1 prediction that needed a minigene assay in five cell lines, the low allergenicity score needs laboratory immune-reactivity testing—and even a clean lab result would be only part of the evidence chain before any consumer-safety claim. 'Confirmed non-allergenic' is exactly the diagnosis-style leap the article warns against.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Correct transfer maps lookup-speeds-triage (P002–P003), score-then-experiment (P004), and score-as-partial-evidence (P005) onto the new domain without cure/safety overclaim.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The article's mechanism transfers cleanly and completely to this unseen scenario, so unseen transfer passes.
